claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructured state with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
A hybrid reduced-order machine-learning and localized finite-element model can predict Young’s modulus of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 within approximately 5–10% of experiment.
The hybrid model can predict yield strength of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 within approximately 5–10% of experiment.
The hybrid model can predict fracture toughness of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 within approximately 5–10% of experiment.
The hybrid model will reduce computational time by at least an order of magnitude relative to full high-fidelity simulations.
The proposed surrogate will be trained on a strategically selected subset of high-fidelity finite-element simulations.
The proposed model will represent both global tensile response and localized stress concentrations and crack-tip mechanics.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and their associated local heterogeneity drive the alloy’s macroscopic elastic and inelastic responses.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and local heterogeneity drive localized fracture mechanisms in HfNbTiVAl10.
High-fidelity finite-element simulations can capture the relevant local stress distributions and crack-initiation events.
Training a surrogate on those finite-element simulations incorporates the physical mechanisms governing tensile and fracture behavior.
A surrogate model can reduce reliance on extensive strict or full-scale calculations.
Physically based yield-strength prediction can require complicated and lengthy calculations, making surrogate modeling more practical for large alloy spaces.
Machine-learning models have shown promise for predicting yield strength in related refractory or multi-principal-element alloy systems.
The cited prior surrogate modeling has shown promise for predicting elasticity in similar systems.
The approach may become unreliable when the target microstructure differs substantially from the training data.
The approach may become unreliable when nonlocal or emergent fracture phenomena are absent from the finite-element training simulations.
Extending surrogate prediction to fracture toughness is more uncertain because toughness depends on highly localized behavior and may be sensitive to conditions outside the training domain.
